title: Development of a Novel Architectural Design Framework for Supporting Occupants' Healthy Circadian Rhythm in Interior Spaces
central_proposition: This research develops a novel architectural design framework to guide architects and lighting designers in creating lighting systems that support occupants' healthy circadian rhythm and overall well-being in interior spaces.

concept_definitions.name: Circadian Rhythm
concept_definitions.definition: A physiological mechanism controlling every human action, including digestion, sleep and waking hours, hormone release, blood pressure, and body temperature, which is an endogenous clock that can be controlled by an outside stimulus like light.

concept_definitions.name: LEDification
concept_definitions.definition: The process of replacing other light bulbs with Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs).

concept_definitions.name: Intelligent Lighting Systems (ILS)
concept_definitions.definition: LED technology incorporated into intelligent buildings to create smart lighting solutions.

concept_definitions.name: Human-Centric Lighting (HCL)
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting design that focuses on improving human mood, relaxation, energy, health, and well-being, closely related to circadian rhythm and biodynamic illumination.

concept_definitions.name: ipRGCs (Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells)
concept_definitions.definition: Specialized cells in the retina that respond to light and play a crucial role in regulating circadian rhythm and melatonin secretion, without contributing to human vision.

concept_definitions.name: CCT (Correlated Color Temperature)
concept_definitions.definition: A metric used to describe the color appearance of a light source, indicating its perceived 'warmth' or 'coolness'.

concept_definitions.name: CRI (Color Rendering Index)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of how accurately a light source illuminates colors compared to a natural light source, on a scale from 0 to 100.

concept_definitions.name: EML (Equivalent Melanopic Lux)
concept_definitions.definition: A metric used to measure the biological impact of light on the human circadian system, weighted to the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs).

concept_definitions.name: CS (Circadian Stimulus)
concept_definitions.definition: A metric that quantifies the circadian impact of light on the human biological system, helping to regulate sleep-wake patterns and overall well-being, with CS ≥ 0.3 at the eye for at least one hour in the early morning being enough to trigger circadian rhythm.

concept_definitions.name: IPD (Integrated Project Delivery)
concept_definitions.definition: A collaborative project delivery method involving early involvement and shared responsibility among all stakeholders to optimize project outcomes, breaking down silos of responsibility.

concept_definitions.name: LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design)
concept_definitions.definition: A rating system developed by the United States Green Building Council to evaluate the sustainability and environmental performance of buildings.

concept_definitions.name: WELL (WELL Building Standard)
concept_definitions.definition: A performance-based system for measuring, certifying, and monitoring features of the built environment that impact human health and well-being, covering eight main areas including light.

concept_definitions.name: BIOS Lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting technologies designed to support human health and well-being by considering the biological impact of light on the circadian system.

concept_definitions.name: EV (Equivalent Vertical Illuminance)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of the amount of light falling on a vertical surface at eye level, relevant to lighting design and its impact on visual perception and the circadian system.

concept_definitions.name: EH (Equivalent Horizontal Illuminance)
concept_definitions.definition: A measure of the amount of light falling on a horizontal surface, such as a desk or table, relevant for visual task performance.

concept_definitions.name: SAD (Seasonal Affective Disorder)
concept_definitions.definition: A disease that changes human mood based on light variations in the seasons, linked to serotonin and melatonin levels.

concept_definitions.name: Melatonin
concept_definitions.definition: A hormone secreted from pineal glands, stimulated by a dark environment perceived by the human eye retina, serving as a robust circadian biomarker.

concept_definitions.name: Circadian Phase Shift
concept_definitions.definition: Changes in the internal body clock, caused by external stimuli, that alter the body’s sleep-wake cycle from the environmental day-night cycle.

concept_definitions.name: Tacit Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge that is hard to learn through written or verbal means, based on personal experience, and difficult to document or transfer except through teacher-student interaction.

concept_definitions.name: Explicit Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge that can be documented and transmitted through different media, being a more formal and easily shareable type of knowledge.

concept_definitions.name: Implicit Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge gained without any conscious effort by the learner, often resulting from explicit knowledge.

concept_definitions.name: Procedural Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge that helps to realize 'how to do something,' consisting of a sequence of interrelated operations based on information received and saved in memory.

concept_definitions.name: Priori Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge that is known without the aid of experience, such as light as a sensory stimulation.

concept_definitions.name: Posteriori Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Knowledge that is derived from specific experience or observation, such as specific lighting needs of a space or people's behavior.

concept_definitions.name: POE (Post-Occupancy Evaluation)
concept_definitions.definition: A specific process used to assess the performance of a building or space after it has been occupied, involving data collection on factors like lighting levels and occupant satisfaction.

concept_definitions.name: VITALS
concept_definitions.definition: An acronym for vertical, intensity, timing, appearance, location, and spectrum, representing key considerations for circadian lighting design.

argument_structure: The research develops an architectural design framework using a qualitative, grounded theory approach. It begins with logical argumentation (literature review) to establish foundational knowledge, followed by immersive case studies to explore and refine design scenarios, and concludes with a focus group presentation to gather expert feedback and finalize the framework.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is that light's spectral quality, intensity, timing, and location impact intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which regulate melatonin secretion and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the master circadian clock. This regulation, in turn, affects physiological processes (sleep-wake cycles, hormone release, body temperature, immune system) and psychological states (mood, alertness, cognitive function). The proposed framework guides designers to manipulate these light characteristics, along with interior design elements and site parameters, to optimize these biological and psychological outcomes, thereby supporting healthy circadian rhythms and overall well-being.

findings.consequent: Impact on immune system
findings.mechanism: Circadian rhythm controls physiological mechanisms including the immune system.
findings.quote: any modification to this clock may have an impact on a person's immune system.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Research by Hall, Rosbash, Young (2017) on fruit flies, Hatori et al. (2017)

findings.consequent: Negative impact on health and well-being
findings.mechanism: Blue light significantly influences human circadian rhythm, and excessive exposure can disrupt it.
findings.empirical_support_cited: European Commission's Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental, and Emerging Risks (SCHEER)

findings.consequent: Psychiatric disorders (depression, anorexia, bulimia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, social anxiety) and affected human mood
findings.mechanism: Serotonin, secreted from the Pineal Gland, stimulates the human body during its wake cycle and is essential for a healthy circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: Low Serotonin levels will affect human mood and will create psychiatric disorders such as depression, anorexia, bulimia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and social anxiety

findings.consequent: Adverse health effects (increased blood sugar, blood pressure, fatigue, weight gain)
findings.mechanism: Cortisol, a stress hormone secreted from the adrenal cortex, is affected by circadian rhythm and high levels are detrimental to health.
findings.quote: High cortisol levels will adversely affect our health by causing an increase in blood sugar and pressure, fatigue, weight gain, etc.

findings.antecedent: Lack of access to natural day/night light cycle
findings.consequent: Affected melatonin secretion and disrupted human sleep-wake cycle
findings.mechanism: The natural cycle of day and night, through sunlight or electric light, is crucial for synchronizing the SCN, which manages melatonin secretion.
findings.quote: the lack of access to the natural cycle of day and night (through sunlight or electric light) will affect the secretion of melatonin hormone in the body and it will adversely affect the human sleep-wake cycle

findings.consequent: Activated circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Human circadian rhythm is very sensitive to short-wavelength (bluer) visible light (446-477 nm), which stimulates photoreception.
findings.quote: Brightness exposure is needed in the morning to activate circadian rhythm

findings.consequent: Tiredness and reduced work effectiveness
findings.mechanism: Chronic sleep debt impacts physiological and cognitive function, leading to fatigue and decreased performance.
findings.quote: People with chronic sleep debt feel permanently tired and are unlikely to work effectively
findings.empirical_support_cited: Lighting Research Center (LRC) research (Blask et al. 2006)

findings.consequent: Higher risk of cancer
findings.mechanism: Melatonin has an oncostatic nature, and its disruption due to shift work can increase cancer risk.
findings.quote: the risk of cancer in shift workers is higher due to changes in their melatonin level compared to people who sleep in the dark at night.

findings.antecedent: Spending time in biologically dark spaces during the day
findings.consequent: Disruption of circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Lack of sufficient light stimulus for ipRGCs in 'biologically dark' zones disrupts circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: people spending a lot of time in those spaces during the day are at risk of disruption of their circadian rhythm

findings.antecedent: Intense artificial light exposure in winter
findings.consequent: Reduced SAD symptoms
findings.mechanism: Light affects serotonin and melatonin levels, which are linked to Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD).
findings.quote: Exposing people with SAD to intense artificial light in winter has helped them reduce symptoms after a few days
findings.empirical_support_cited: Lewy et al. (1982), Meesters et al. (2016)

findings.antecedent: Improved circadian rhythmicity (melatonin therapy, physical activity)
findings.consequent: Positive effect on Alzheimer's disease and aging process
findings.mechanism: Circadian rhythm regulates various physiological functions that are implicated in Alzheimer's and aging.
findings.quote: Improved circadian rhythmicity through melatonin therapy and physical activity will positively affect Alzheimer's disease and the aging process

findings.antecedent: Natural light and windows in learning environments
findings.consequent: Positive psychophysiological and performance effects
findings.mechanism: Natural light supports circadian rhythm, mood, and visual comfort, which are beneficial for learning.
findings.quote: natural light and the presence of windows in learning environments have positive psychophysiological and performance effects

findings.consequent: More beneficial visual acuity for elementary school children
findings.mechanism: Higher CCT (cooler light) can enhance visual performance and alertness.
findings.quote: a continuous level of illuminance on a school desk with CCT of 5500 K was shown to be more beneficial to elementary school kids' visual acuity than CCT of 3600 K

findings.antecedent: Higher illuminance (1060 lux vs 300 lux) and higher CCT (5800 K vs 4000 K)
findings.consequent: Fewer mistakes and improved reading abilities in students
findings.mechanism: Optimal light levels and CCT support cognitive performance and reduce errors.
findings.quote: in the classroom with a 1060 lux illuminance level and a CCT of 5800 K, students made fewer mistakes and had improvements in their reading abilities, compared to the other classroom with 300 lux illuminance level and CCT of 4000 K

findings.antecedent: Sleeping less than 8 hours, noisy room with lights on
findings.consequent: Increased sleep bruxism in children
findings.mechanism: Sleep deprivation and environmental disturbances (noise, light) disrupt sleep quality, leading to bruxism.
findings.quote: children who slept less than 8 hours at night were more likely to suffer sleep bruxism, and it was more common among children sleeping in a noisy room with lights on

findings.antecedent: Long-term psychological and physical stress, lack of sleep, night or sound disturbances
findings.consequent: Night terror
findings.mechanism: These factors disrupt sleep patterns and can trigger night terrors.
findings.quote: situations of long-term psychological and physical stress, lack of sleep, or any night or sound disturbances at night

findings.consequent: Improved sleep onset and maintenance
findings.mechanism: Melatonin regulates sleep-wake cycles, and low doses can aid in initiating and maintaining sleep.
findings.quote: low-dose melatonin therapy for people having insomnia improves their sleep onset and maintenance.

findings.consequent: Side effects and adversely affected circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Excessive melatonin can disrupt the body's natural rhythm, leading to adverse effects.
findings.quote: high melatonin doses (over 0.3 mg) have side effects and adversely affect their circadian rhythm

findings.antecedent: Evening exposure to blue short wavelengths from screens
findings.consequent: Sleep disorders
findings.mechanism: Blue light suppresses melatonin and delays the circadian phase, interfering with sleep.
findings.quote: blue short wavelengths in television or tablet screens if used in the evening can cause sleep disorders.

findings.consequent: Adverse effects on animal health
findings.mechanism: Blue light impacts circadian rhythm in animals, leading to negative health outcomes.
findings.quote: Blue light from electric light can adversely affect animals’ health as well.
findings.empirical_support_cited: European Commission's Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental, and Emerging Risks (SCHEER)

findings.antecedent: Dynamic LED lighting system (in ISS Crew Quarters)
findings.consequent: Significant difference in melatonin assay and suppression
findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting can regulate circadian rhythm by adjusting light characteristics over time.
findings.quote: melatonin assay and suppression test results showed a significant difference

findings.consequent: Circadian action factor of constant LED light source
findings.mechanism: Age-related changes in retinal illuminance and circadian rhythm sensitivity reduce the circadian action factor.
findings.quote: the circadian action factor of a constant LED light source decreases as age increases

findings.consequent: Retinal illuminance, circadian rhythm, blue light hazard
findings.mechanism: Age-related changes in the eye and central nervous system lead to a decrease in these factors.
findings.quote: the change in retinal illuminance, circadian rhythm, and blue light hazard will change with age. These factors decrease as a person ages

findings.consequent: Decreased nocturnal melatonin concentration
findings.mechanism: Age-related changes in pineal gland function lead to reduced melatonin production at night.
findings.quote: When human ages nocturnal melatonin concentration will decrease.

findings.consequent: Wandering and agitation in Alzheimer's patients
findings.mechanism: Melatonin affects neurobehavioral patterns, influencing symptoms like wandering and agitation.
findings.quote: Melatonin levels can also affect wandering and agitation in patients having Alzheimer's.

findings.antecedent: Melatonin treatment (for children with developmental disabilities)
findings.consequent: Increased sleep duration and decreased sleep latency
findings.mechanism: Melatonin regulates sleep, and its treatment can correct abnormal levels in children with developmental disabilities.
findings.quote: melatonin treatment on a group of children with developmental disabilities and reported a positive impact and an increase in sleep duration and a decrease in sleep latency

findings.antecedent: Artificial light source spectral quality (closer to natural light spectrum)
findings.consequent: Enhancement in human health
findings.mechanism: A light spectrum closer to natural light supports physiological processes and overall human health.
findings.quote: the closer an artificial light source gets to the standard light spectrum the more enhancement in human health will happen

findings.consequent: Phase advance the circadian clock
findings.mechanism: Light exposure in the early morning resets the biological clock, promoting circadian resetting.
findings.quote: Enough daylight illuminance can serve to phase advance the clock in the majority of people.

findings.consequent: Increased subjective alertness
findings.mechanism: Light can have alerting effects independent of circadian phase shifting, enhancing subjective alertness.
findings.quote: High levels of daylight illuminance may lead to increased levels of subjective alertness without exerting substantial phase-shifting effects on the clock.

findings.consequent: Disruption of natural wake-sleep cycle
findings.mechanism: Light at night suppresses melatonin and delays the circadian phase, interfering with natural sleep patterns.
findings.quote: Daylight exposure that might trigger the non-visual effect is to be avoided so as not to disrupt the natural wake-sleep cycle.

findings.consequent: Human melatonin secretion, human health, immune system, work efficiency
findings.mechanism: Light directly impacts melatonin, which in turn affects health and performance.
findings.quote: Human melatonin secretion is highly affected by the color and intensity of environmental light. This can affect human health, the immune system, and work efficiency.

findings.consequent: Associated moods/emotions (stimulating, exciting, disturbing, sad, cheerful, joyful, tender, soothing, calm, peaceful, serene, dignified, stately)
findings.mechanism: Psychological associations with color are culturally and individually influenced, leading to specific emotional responses.
findings.quote: Most participants associated red with adjectives such as stimulating and exciting, orange with disturbing and sad, and yellow with “cheerful and joyful”. On the other hand, blue was tender, soothing, calm, peaceful, and serene, and purple was dignified and stately

findings.consequent: Color-emotion associations
findings.mechanism: Sociocultural and developmental factors shape color perception and emotional response.
findings.quote: There is a body of literature suggesting that there is a difference between the color and associated emotions of people from different cultures, backgrounds, and age groups.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hupka et al. (1997), Boyatzis and Varghese (1994), Bluyssen et al. (2019)

findings.consequent: Increased self-control, awareness, motivation for good behaviors
findings.mechanism: Bright light enhances mental alertness and cognitive control.
findings.quote: participants had more control over their behavior in a bright environment than in a dim room. It can also increase their awareness and motivation toward having good behaviors in society

findings.consequent: Better self-control, lower cognitive depletion
findings.mechanism: Optimal light conditions support cognitive resources and reduce mental fatigue.
findings.quote: in warmer (4000K) and brighter ambient, participants had better self-control compared to a dim environment. Warm bright and cool dark lighting conditions resulted in lower cognitive depletion, whereas dim warm and bright cool lighting resulted in higher cognitive depletion.

findings.consequent: Healthier food choices (mediated by mental alertness)
findings.mechanism: Ambient light increases mental alertness, influencing decision-making towards healthier options.
findings.quote: customers tend to choose a healthier option in a bright environment. It is because of the effect of ambient light on mental alertness which in turn affects people's food choices

findings.consequent: Improved comfort and communication between counselor and client
findings.mechanism: Dim light creates a more relaxed and intimate atmosphere, facilitating open communication.
findings.quote: both counselor and client felt better in a dim room and could speak more with each other.

findings.consequent: Human perception, space ambience, cognitive and emotional responses
findings.mechanism: Light acts as a psychocognitive tool, shaping perception and emotion.
findings.quote: Light can drive human perception through the induction of “cognitive and emotional responses”.

findings.consequent: Increased emotional responses
findings.mechanism: Multisensory integration enhances affective experience.
findings.quote: Adding other media to light such as music can increase emotional responses.

findings.consequent: Affected ambient temperature perception, induced tactile sensation
findings.mechanism: Cross-modal sensory effects, where visual input influences thermal and tactile perception.
findings.quote: Colored light can also affect the ambient temperature and induce tactile sensation in humans

findings.consequent: Faster emotional responses, increased alertness
findings.mechanism: High light levels stimulate arousal systems, leading to quicker emotional processing and heightened alertness.
findings.quote: High levels of light cause faster emotional responses and increase alertness

findings.consequent: Sensory deprivation (Sendep effect)
findings.mechanism: Lack of sensory variation leads to perceptual monotony and sensory deprivation.
findings.quote: Being exposed to constant uniform light for a long time can cause sensory deprivation or the Sendep effect.

findings.consequent: Prevention of SAD, support for circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Lighting directly influences physiological and psychological health by regulating circadian rhythms and mood.
findings.quote: Paying attention to human health and providing them with a healthy lighting system to prevent SAD and support their circadian rhythm is also important and trending

findings.consequent: Failure to stimulate occupants' circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: LEED's focus on average daylight in limited areas does not ensure sufficient light exposure for circadian entrainment in all occupied spaces.
findings.quote: LEED certificate requires daylighting of only a portion of regularly occupied areas (55% or 75% of floor area), and they do not delineate the rest. This causes a failure to stimulate occupants' circadian rhythm

findings.antecedent: Sleep-related problems (nocturnal awakening, multiple naps, difficulty sleeping) in elderly
findings.consequent: Adverse effects on health and immunity
findings.mechanism: Sleep disruption impacts physiological regulation and immune function, leading to poorer health outcomes.
findings.quote: The researcher believes that the biggest problems of elderly are sleep-related. They suffer from nocturnal awakening, having multiple naps during the day, and difficulty going to sleep at night. These problems will adversely affect their health and immunity.

findings.antecedent: Light signals (LED strips on door jambs) at night
findings.consequent: Facilitated orientation, improved movement control in low-light situations
findings.mechanism: Visual cues provide spatial guidance without disrupting circadian rhythm, aiding navigation in dim conditions.
findings.quote: used light signals such as LED strips on door jambs to facilitate their sense of orientation at night. The presence of light signals can help them even in a low-light situation.

findings.antecedent: Innovative lighting program and control (Philips Lighting)
findings.consequent: 40% more energy-efficient patient suite, addressed visual and non-visual needs
findings.mechanism: Integrated design considering both visual comfort and circadian regulation optimizes lighting performance and energy use.
findings.quote: The outcome was a lighting solution for a 40% more energy-efficient patient suite that could answer all visual and non-visual needs of patients and healthcare workers.

findings.antecedent: Insufficient daylight/artificial light during the day
findings.consequent: Lack of melatonin suppression, drowsiness, depression
findings.mechanism: Light regulates melatonin secretion; insufficient daytime light prevents natural suppression, leading to drowsiness and mood issues.
findings.quote: daylight or artificial light during the day, natural suppression of Melatonin would not occur and will create a sense of drowsiness and depression.

findings.antecedent: High-intensity blue light exposure at night
findings.consequent: Alertness at night
findings.mechanism: Blue light stimulates ipRGCs, suppressing melatonin and promoting alertness, even at night.
findings.quote: being exposed to high-intensity light (especially in the blue range) will cause alertness at night.

findings.antecedent: Light source intensity and spectral quality
findings.consequent: Occupants' circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Light characteristics directly influence circadian regulation through ipRGCs.
findings.quote: Light source intensity and spectral quality will affect occupants’ circadian rhythm, so architects and lighting designers play a very important role in designing spaces with the proper electric lighting system in buildings.

findings.consequent: Difficulty and cost of making changes
findings.mechanism: Design decisions become more entrenched and interdependent over time, making late-stage modifications harder and more expensive.
findings.quote: As we move forward in this process, making changes will become harder and more costly.

findings.antecedent: Intelligence (e.g., circadian lighting considerations) inserted in early design stages
findings.consequent: Better design results
findings.mechanism: Early integration allows for fundamental design decisions to be made effectively and with less cost.
findings.quote: To gain better results, intelligence should be inserted in all different stages of design, including the schematic design stage

findings.consequent: Collaboration among group members, breakdown of silos
findings.mechanism: IPD fosters shared goals and continuous communication among diverse stakeholders.
findings.quote: IPD breaks down the silos of responsibility and requires different group members to closely collaborate through different stages of the project.

findings.consequent: Common goal of project success, emphasis on project value
findings.mechanism: IPD aligns stakeholder interests towards project success and value over individual cost concerns.
findings.quote: In this method, group members have a common goal which is the project's success and what they emphasize is the project value instead of its cost.

findings.antecedent: Lack of comprehensive framework for circadian lighting design
findings.consequent: Need for a comprehensive framework
findings.mechanism: Existing knowledge is fragmented, requiring a structured approach to guide designers.
findings.quote: Based on the results from the mentioned studies, there is a need for a comprehensive and clear architectural design framework that would address the required knowledge, steps, and proper tools for circadian lighting design in buildings.

findings.antecedent: Previous studies on circadian lighting design
findings.consequent: Missing elements affecting non-visual light effects on humans
findings.mechanism: Incomplete understanding of all influencing factors in circadian lighting design.
findings.quote: In previous studies on circadian lighting design, many elements that would affect the non-visual effect of light on human are missing.

findings.consequent: Supported occupant health, regulated healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Daylight provides natural light cues essential for circadian entrainment and overall well-being.
findings.quote: Having enough access to daylight in the building will support the occupants’ health by regulating their healthy circadian rhythm.

findings.consequent: Proper light color throughout the day
findings.mechanism: Tunable LEDs allow dynamic adjustment of light spectral quality to mimic natural daylight patterns.
findings.quote: Studies suggest using tunable LED sources to provide proper light color throughout the day.

findings.consequent: Physiological reactions
findings.mechanism: Mind-body connection, where emotional responses triggered by color can induce physiological changes.
findings.quote: The psychological reaction caused by color can lead to physiological reactions too

findings.consequent: Consumers' perception of goods
findings.mechanism: Light color influences aesthetic judgment and cognitive associations with products.
findings.quote: Studies show that light color affects consumers' perception of goods

findings.consequent: People's perception of fabric (price, age, texture)
findings.mechanism: CCT influences color appearance and associated material properties, altering perception.
findings.quote: different light sources with different CCTs were used to illuminate pieces of fabric and the results showed that it affected people’s perception of fabric price, being old or new, soft or rigid, and so forth.

findings.consequent: Modified experienced SPD in space
findings.mechanism: Materials selectively absorb and reflect wavelengths, altering the spectral composition of light in a space.
findings.quote: As colored walls absorb some of the SPD and reflect others, our experienced SPD is further modified.

findings.consequent: Supported healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Color influences the spectral composition of light reaching the eye, affecting ipRGCs and thus circadian regulation.
findings.quote: Color should support human (or animals') healthy circadian rhythm as well.

findings.consequent: Stimulation of hypothalamic midbrain area, affected endocrine system
findings.mechanism: Direct neural pathway from the retina to brain regions controlling hormones and the endocrine system.
findings.quote: The light carried by the human optic pathway stimulates the hypothalamic midbrain area. This area affects and controls the endocrine system of the human body

findings.consequent: Biological reactions (circadian rhythm, hormone secretions)
findings.mechanism: Innate physiological responses to light/color, influencing circadian rhythm and hormone regulation.
findings.quote: Other biological effects that relate to human circadian rhythm and hormone secretions are widely discussed in the previous chapter. This section of the pyramid is beyond human control.

findings.antecedent: Color hues (blue, blue-green, green, yellow, orange, red, red-violet)
findings.consequent: Associated moods/emotions (peace, tranquility, happiness, love)
findings.mechanism: Psychological associations with color, influenced by cultural and individual experiences.
findings.quote: colors such as blue, blue-green, and green with peace and tranquility, more than 63% associated yellow and orange with happiness, and 81% of participants associated red and red-violet with love.

findings.consequent: Interference with healthcare worker performance, increased patient anxiety
findings.mechanism: Visual overstimulation or negative psychological associations can impair cognitive function and increase stress.
findings.quote: Using too many sharp colors should also be avoided since it can interfere with the performance of healthcare workers and increase patient anxiety over the long term.

findings.consequent: Reduced patient stress, reduced hospital stay duration
findings.mechanism: Nature exposure and natural light promote stress recovery and healing processes.
findings.quote: Daylight reduces stress in patients and the days they need to spend in the hospital
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hua, Oswald, and Yang (2011), Iyendo and Alibaba (2014)

findings.consequent: Positive impact on patient/staff well-being, faster healing process
findings.mechanism: Natural light supports circadian rhythm, mood, and stress recovery, contributing to overall well-being and healing.
findings.quote: The use of daylighting in the hospital environment positively impacts patients' and staff's well-being. It can also help with a faster healing process
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hua, Oswald, and Yang (2011), Iyendo and Alibaba (2014)

findings.consequent: Reduced medical error rate
findings.mechanism: Adequate light levels improve visual acuity and alertness, reducing the likelihood of errors.
findings.quote: Studies show that a light level of 1500 lux inside buildings can reduce the medical error rate compared to lower intensities

findings.antecedent: Irregular 24h lighting, bright lights in evening, insufficient morning light
findings.consequent: Affected human health, disrupted circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Disruption of the natural light-dark cycle interferes with circadian entrainment, leading to negative health outcomes.
findings.quote: irregular 24h lighting can affect human health by disrupting the circadian rhythm. However, being exposed to bright lights in the evening and insufficient morning light is common in the healthcare environment.

findings.antecedent: Intervention lighting (2 hours bright light in morning, low light at night)
findings.consequent: Increased patient sleep duration (by 29 minutes)
findings.mechanism: Circadian-effective lighting promotes healthy sleep-wake cycles by providing appropriate light cues.
findings.quote: in the rooms with intervention lighting, patients' sleep duration increased by 29 minutes.

findings.consequent: Disrupted circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Melanopsin-sensitive ipRGCs are highly responsive to light at night, suppressing melatonin and disrupting circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: High Light exposure in the evening and night can disrupt circadian rhythm and is mostly affected by melanopsin rather than photopic light. It means that controlling the light color is very important in minimizing the negative impacts of night light

findings.consequent: Improved nurse performance
findings.mechanism: CECL provides appropriate lighting for tasks and circadian support, enhancing cognitive function and alertness.
findings.quote: nurses could perform better in hospitals incorporating CECL lighting system.

findings.consequent: Patient awareness/perception of good lighting
findings.mechanism: Lighting quality contributes to overall environmental perception and comfort, even in severe illness.
findings.quote: patients are often aware of the good lighting even if they are suffering from severe illness and critical treatments

findings.consequent: Suppressed melatonin production in the morning
findings.mechanism: LEDs can provide high-intensity blue-enriched light, effectively stimulating ipRGCs for melatonin suppression.
findings.quote: LED also successfully produced sufficient light to suppress melatonin production in the morning

findings.antecedent: Combination of warm and cold hues distributed in multiple zones
findings.consequent: Patient preference
findings.mechanism: Provides visual variety and adaptability to different needs and tasks, enhancing comfort and preference.
findings.quote: most of them preferred a combination of warm and cold hues that were distributed in multiple zones in the room rather than one focused over the headlight.

findings.consequent: Discomfort
findings.mechanism: Cooler light can be perceived as harsh or unnatural in certain contexts, leading to visual discomfort.
findings.quote: CCTs higher than 5000K were uncomfortable compared to warmer ones

findings.antecedent: Lighting design considering human circadian system needs (in offices)
findings.consequent: Enhanced worker mood, boosted job alertness, improved nighttime sleep, mitigated chronic health risks
findings.mechanism: Circadian-effective lighting regulates physiological and psychological states, leading to improved well-being and performance.
findings.quote: lighting design that takes into account the needs of the human circadian system can enhance workers' overall mood, boost job alertness without disrupting circadian entrainment, improve nighttime sleep, and mitigate the risks of chronic health issues that are linked to disruptions in the circadian system.

findings.antecedent: High-intensity blue light during the day (in healthcare)
findings.consequent: Improved nurse/patient performance and productivity
findings.mechanism: Blue light promotes alertness and cognitive function during the day, enhancing performance.
findings.quote: strategic use of high-intensity blue light during the day can benefit both nurses and patients by improving performance and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Warmer, lower-intensity lighting at night (in nurse stations)
findings.consequent: Supported circadian rhythm (by avoiding disruption)
findings.mechanism: Reduces melatonin suppression at night, maintaining circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: In the evening and at night, nurse stations can be illuminated with warmer, lower-intensity lighting, and task lighting can be provided as needed.

findings.antecedent: Fully darkened rooms with safety lights at night (for patients)
findings.consequent: Supported sleep, safe navigation
findings.mechanism: Darkness promotes melatonin production for sleep; safety lights provide minimal visual cues without circadian disruption.
findings.quote: Patients, on the other hand, should be able to sleep in fully darkened rooms with safety lights available to ensure safe navigation.

findings.consequent: Changes in eye/CNS, adverse effects on daily functioning, health, well-being, visual/non-visual light responses
findings.mechanism: Age-related physiological deterioration impacts sensory and neurological systems.
findings.quote: The aging process can cause changes in the eye and central nervous system that may have adverse effects on daily functioning, overall health, and well-being, as well as the visual and non-visual systems' responses to light

findings.consequent: Decreased visual field size, increased absolute threshold luminance, reduced visual activity, decreased contrast sensitivity, increased glare sensitivity, decreased color discrimination
findings.mechanism: Age-related changes in ocular and neural visual processing lead to various visual impairments.
findings.quote: Elderly individuals often exhibit a decrease in visual field size, an increase in absolute threshold luminance, a reduction in visual activity, a decrease in contrast sensitivity, an increased sensitivity to glare, and a decrease in color discrimination ability

findings.antecedent: Certain lighting conditions (for children with special needs)
findings.consequent: Improved daytime performance, good night sleep
findings.mechanism: Tailored lighting supports their specific physiological and behavioral needs, optimizing performance and sleep.
findings.quote: children with special needs require certain lighting conditions to help them perform better during the day and have a good night sleep

findings.antecedent: High levels of blue light during the day
findings.consequent: Increased alertness
findings.mechanism: Blue light stimulates ipRGCs, promoting wakefulness and cognitive function.
findings.quote: light with high levels of blue, especially during the day, can increase alertness.

findings.antecedent: Lower or warmer light levels at night
findings.consequent: Beneficial for melatonin production
findings.mechanism: Reduces suppression of melatonin, supporting natural sleep cycles.
findings.quote: lower or warmer light levels are beneficial for melatonin production at night.

findings.antecedent: Flicker-free, scattered light with high CRI
findings.consequent: Better vision
findings.mechanism: Reduces visual discomfort and enhances color perception, improving visual quality.
findings.quote: To ensure better vision, it is recommended to use flicker-free, scattered light with high color rendering index (CRI).

findings.consequent: Welcoming and comfortable environment
findings.mechanism: Psychological associations with warm colors evoke feelings of comfort and welcome.
findings.quote: warm interior colors can be used to create a welcoming and comfortable environment.

findings.antecedent: Strategically designed lighting system (mimicking natural daylight changes)
findings.consequent: Improved student mood, energy levels, cognitive function
findings.mechanism: Supports circadian rhythm and psychological well-being by providing appropriate light cues throughout the day.
findings.quote: By strategically designing the lighting system to mimic the natural changes in daylight, students can experience improved mood, energy levels, and cognitive function.

findings.antecedent: High levels of blue light during the day
findings.consequent: Increased alertness and productivity
findings.mechanism: Blue light stimulates ipRGCs, promoting wakefulness and cognitive function.
findings.quote: High levels of blue light during the day can increase alertness and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Minimized blue light exposure during evening hours
findings.consequent: Improved cognitive performance during the day, restful sleep at night
findings.mechanism: Prevents melatonin suppression and circadian disruption at night, supporting healthy sleep and daytime cognitive function.
findings.quote: minimizing exposure to blue light during the evening hours... students can experience improved cognitive performance during the day while also getting the restful sleep they need at night.

findings.antecedent: Light coming from below the horizon
findings.consequent: Impact on circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: ipRGCs are more sensitive to light from above the horizon, making light from below less impactful on circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: light coming from below the horizon does not have an impact on our circadian rhythm, as opposed to light from above the horizon

findings.consequent: Stimulation of circadian system
findings.mechanism: The peak spectral sensitivity of the human circadian system is around 460 nm, making short wavelengths most effective.
findings.quote: short-wavelength light with a range of 465-475 nm is most effective in stimulating the circadian system.

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength light (compared to longer wavelength) experienced in the evening
findings.consequent: Greater impact on suppressing melatonin, delaying circadian phase
findings.mechanism: Blue light is more potent for circadian disruption at night due to ipRGCs sensitivity.
findings.quote: Compared to longer wavelength (warmer) light, short-wavelength light has a greater impact on suppressing melatonin and delaying circadian phase if experienced in the evening.

findings.consequent: Impact on melatonin suppression or circadian phase
findings.mechanism: ipRGCs are less sensitive to longer wavelengths, resulting in minimal effect on circadian regulation.
findings.quote: Long-wavelength light, on the other hand, has little impact on suppressing melatonin or affecting circadian phase.

findings.consequent: Promoted alertness without disrupting circadian system
findings.mechanism: Provides visual stimulation and alertness without strong melanopic impact, preserving circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: long-wavelength light is particularly useful in promoting alertness during the afternoon and evening without disrupting the circadian system
findings.empirical_support_cited: Mariana G. Figueiro et al. (2009); Plitnick et al. (2010)

findings.antecedent: LEED requirements (daylight in perimeter zones, glare/flicker control, flicker-free equipment, CRI >= 80, R9 >= 50)
findings.consequent: Adequate daylight, optimal indoor lighting, visual comfort
findings.mechanism: LEED sets standards for visual quality and environmental performance.
findings.quote: LEED mandates that regularly occupied areas of a building's perimeter zone receive adequate levels of daylight, while also taking into account issues of glare and flicker. To ensure optimal indoor lighting, LEED also requires the use of flicker-free equipment with a Color Rendering Index (CRI) of 80 or higher and an R9 value of at least 50 for electric lights

findings.antecedent: WELL Standard requirement (>= 200 EML at eye level for >= 4 hours, 9 AM - 1 PM)
findings.consequent: Maintained healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Specific EML levels at critical times entrain the circadian clock.
findings.quote: At least 200 equivalent melanopic lux is present at 75% or more of the workstations, as measured on the vertical plane looking forward, 1.2 m [4 ft] above the completed floor. This light intensity is present every day through the year for at least the hours between 9:00 AM and 1:00 PM and may include daylight.

findings.antecedent: WELL Standard requirement (>= 150 EML from electric lights at eye level)
findings.consequent: Maintained healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Provides sufficient melanopic stimulus from artificial sources to support circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: Electric lights at all workstations must maintain illumination of at least 150 equivalent melanopic lux on the vertical plane looking forward.

findings.antecedent: WELL Standard requirement (>= 200 EML during daylight in living environments)
findings.consequent: Maintained healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Ensures adequate melanopic stimulus in residential settings to support circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: At least 200 equivalent melanopic lux during the daylight, as measured facing the wall in the middle of the space, 1.2 m (4 ft) above the completed floor. Although they can independently reach these settings, the lights may be lowered when there is daylight present.

findings.antecedent: WELL Standard requirement (<= 50 EML at night in living environments)
findings.consequent: Supported healthy circadian rhythm (by avoiding disruption)
findings.mechanism: Minimizes melatonin suppression at night, which is crucial for healthy sleep and circadian regulation.
findings.quote: As measured 0.76 m [30 inches] above the completed floor at night, lights give no more than 50 equivalent melanopic lux.

findings.antecedent: Site analysis (nearby buildings, foliage, building orientation)
findings.consequent: Daylight availability, natural light access
findings.mechanism: External factors like obstructions and orientation create shadows and block natural light.
findings.quote: potential factors that may limit daylight availability, such as nearby buildings and foliage, should be identified. Furthermore, the impact of the building's orientation on natural light access should be evaluated.

findings.antecedent: Room color (light blue, aquamarine vs. red, orange)
findings.consequent: Melanopic lux
findings.mechanism: Different colors reflect different spectral power distributions, affecting the melanopic response of ipRGCs.
findings.quote: room colors with the greatest melanopic lux are light blue (Munsell 10P 8/4) and Dupont Aquamarine 24, whereas the room colors with the lowest melanopic lux are Dupont Red 2 and Dupont Orange 6.

findings.antecedent: Cold paint colors + low CCT and intensity light source
findings.consequent: Melanopic lux levels (< 50)
findings.mechanism: Reduced light intensity can counteract the melanopic impact of cooler colors, allowing them to meet nighttime EML thresholds.
findings.quote: even cold paint colors, when combined with a light source with a lower CCT and intensity, may maintain melanopic lux levels of less than 50, which is permitted by the WELL Building Standard.

findings.consequent: Lower melanopic lux (compared to green, blue)
findings.mechanism: Warmer colors reflect less blue light, reducing the melanopic stimulus.
findings.quote: warmer room colors like red and orange have lower melanopic lux than cold colors such as green and blue.

findings.antecedent: Interior space color, light SPD, light intensity
findings.consequent: Quantity of melanopic lux
findings.mechanism: These factors determine the spectral composition and intensity of light reaching ipRGCs, directly influencing melanopic lux.
findings.quote: Both study findings show that the quantity of melanopic lux is influenced by interior space color, as well as light SPD and intensity.

findings.consequent: Healthy circadian rhythm, better sleep at night (by reducing melatonin suppression)
findings.mechanism: Warmer colors have lower melanopic lux, which is beneficial at night for melatonin production.
findings.quote: warm colors like red or orange might encourage a healthy circadian rhythm and help inhabitants sleep better at night by reducing melatonin suppression.

findings.consequent: Greater photopic and melanopic lux
findings.mechanism: White surfaces reflect a broad spectrum of light, including blue wavelengths, leading to higher lux values.
findings.quote: white walls have a greater photopic and melanopic lux owing to their high reflectivity, therefore designers should use caution while utilizing this hue.

findings.consequent: Increased melanopic lux, circadian disturbance (at night)
findings.mechanism: Cooler colors reflect more blue light, which strongly stimulates ipRGCs, leading to undesirable melanopic lux at night.
findings.quote: Contrary to popular belief, colors viewed as cooler (blue/violet) result in increased melanopic lux, which is undesirable at night and may cause a circadian disturbance.

findings.consequent: Counterbalanced negative effects of paint color/CCT on melanopic lux, ability to select cooler colors while maintaining safe melanopic lux
findings.mechanism: Intensity is a primary driver of melanopic response; reducing it allows for more flexibility with color choices at night.
findings.quote: The reduced nighttime light intensity can help counterbalance the negative effects of paint color and light source CCT on human melanopic lux. Interior designers can lower light intensity to select cooler colors while maintaining a safe level of melanopic lux.

findings.consequent: Altered impact of light source SPD and intensity
findings.mechanism: Paint colors modify the reflected light spectrum, changing the effective SPD and intensity in the space.
findings.quote: Designers may alter the impact of light source SPD and intensity by using different paint colors.

findings.consequent: Failure to ensure enough daylight for each space
findings.mechanism: Aggregated metrics do not capture localized light distribution, leading to deficiencies in specific areas.
findings.quote: A shortcoming of the LEED daylight analysis is that it only uses the average daylight percentage of the whole building and fails to analyze each space to ensure everyone gets enough daylight.

findings.antecedent: Spaces shadowed by adjacent buildings/vegetation/structures or north-oriented with limited openings
findings.consequent: Deficient daylight, need for additional daylighting development to support circadian rhythms
findings.mechanism: Obstructions and orientation limit natural light access, leading to insufficient circadian stimulus.
findings.quote: Such spaces are usually shadowed by adjacent buildings, vegetation or structures, or they may be oriented towards the north with limited openings for natural light. By prioritizing these spaces in our analysis, we can identify areas that required additional daylighting development to support the circadian rhythms of occupants.

findings.antecedent: Inclusion of circadian lighting design from beginning of design process
findings.consequent: Effective design, enhanced patient well-being
findings.mechanism: Early integration allows for fundamental design decisions to support circadian health and well-being.
findings.quote: it is critical to include circadian lighting design from the beginning of the design process.

findings.consequent: Does not guarantee requisite light amounts for every space
findings.mechanism: LEED metrics are often average-based and may not capture localized deficiencies in light distribution.
findings.quote: the LEED daylight model does not guarantee that every space has access to the requisite amounts of light.

findings.antecedent: Proper circadian lighting design (in behavioral healthcare)
findings.consequent: Enhanced patient well-being
findings.mechanism: Supports physiological and psychological health in vulnerable populations.
findings.quote: Proper lighting design may enhance patient well-being.

findings.antecedent: Circadian lighting design incorporated throughout design process
findings.consequent: Ample opportunities to make changes, supported health and well-being
findings.mechanism: Continuous consideration allows for iterative refinement and optimization of design elements for health outcomes.
findings.quote: circadian lighting design can be incorporated throughout the design process, providing ample opportunities to make changes that support health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: Lack of education/prioritization of sustainability (or health/well-being in design)
findings.consequent: Lack of knowledge/ability to implement sustainable practices, insufficient attention to sustainability goals
findings.mechanism: Educational and client engagement gaps hinder the effective implementation of design concepts.
findings.quote: sustainability is often not discussed for more than ten minutes in any project. Secondly, architects receive little to no education on sustainability, resulting in a lack of knowledge and ability to implement sustainable practices. Lastly, many clients do not prioritize sustainability and may not even recycle. It is crucial to educate and remind clients of their project goals regarding sustainability to ensure that it is given the attention it deserves. This can be the same with concepts such as health and well-being in design.

findings.consequent: Changed melanopic lux, affected circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Light color directly influences ipRGCs sensitivity and melatonin suppression, thereby impacting circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: changing the light color at night can change the melanopic lux and consequently affect circadian rhythm.

findings.antecedent: Dynamic patient room color (colder hues in morning, warmer in evening)
findings.consequent: Supported healthy circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Mimics natural daylight cycle, providing stimulating light in the morning and non-stimulating light in the evening.
findings.quote: patient room color can change throughout the day and start from colder hues such as blue, cyan, and green in the morning, and move to warmer tones such as yellow, orange, and red in the evening.

findings.consequent: Melanopic lux > 50 (unacceptable by WELL)
findings.mechanism: These colors reflect more blue light, exceeding the recommended threshold for nighttime melanopic suppression.
findings.quote: melanopic lux goes over 50 as we move to green and colder colors, falling in the unacceptable range by the WELL Building Standard.

findings.consequent: Person's access to light, circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: These factors influence the amount and spectral quality of light reaching the eye, affecting circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: interior design and sitting orientation might also alter a person's access to light. This can either support or disrupt their circadian rhythm.

findings.consequent: Light exposure, light intensity variations, circadian rhythm disturbance
findings.mechanism: Seating orientation affects direct access to natural light, influencing the quantity and variability of light received.
findings.quote: The individual sitting closest to the skylight is exposed to higher amounts of light and feels more variations in light intensity. The individual sitting backward has lower light levels and may have a disturbance in their circadian rhythm.

findings.consequent: Negative impact on circadian rhythm
findings.mechanism: Cooler hues often contain more blue light, which can disrupt circadian rhythm, especially at night, despite their calming psychological effect.
findings.quote: While people may find cooler hues more calming, they can have a negative impact on their circadian rhythm.

findings.consequent: Needed for circadian stimulus throughout the day
findings.mechanism: Despite preference, bright cool light (blue-enriched) is essential for daytime circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: people may dislike bright cool light, but they need pulses of it throughout the day, especially if they spend most of their time indoors.

findings.consequent: Increased circadian stimulus from natural light, increased energy loss, increased glare
findings.mechanism: Larger openings allow more light for circadian entrainment but also increase heat transfer and potential for glare.
findings.quote: A larger window may increase the circadian stimulus from natural light, but it can also cause energy loss and glare.

findings.antecedent: Designing for typical biological response (without considering individual preference)
findings.consequent: Desired outcome may not come to fruition
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and preference can override generalized biological responses, leading to suboptimal outcomes.
findings.quote: If we design for a typical biological response but individual preference has a large impact the desired outcome may not come to fruition.

findings.antecedent: Individual override choice (allowing selection counter to biological response)
findings.consequent: Disrupted circadian rhythm (unknowingly)
findings.mechanism: Personal preference may lead to choices that negatively impact physiological regulation, even if unintended.
findings.quote: If individual override choice is allowed, then the individual may select a scheme which is counter to biological response (if biological response is more dominant) and disrupt their own rhythm unknowingly.

findings.consequent: More efficient space use, reduced need for extensive training
findings.mechanism: Intuitive design reduces cognitive load and the learning curve for users.
findings.quote: good design can lead people to use the space more efficiently, thus reducing the need for extensive training.

findings.antecedent: BIOS desk lamps (targeted lighting, glare reduction)
findings.consequent: Improved overall workspace environment, optimal productivity, reduced eye strain and fatigue
findings.mechanism: Provides appropriate light for visual tasks and circadian needs while minimizing discomfort.
findings.quote: BIOS desk lamps have been designed to provide targeted lighting to both the work plane and the eyes while also reducing glare from computer screens. This innovative lighting solution can help improve the overall workspace environment, making it conducive for optimal productivity and reducing eye strain and fatigue.

findings.antecedent: Good access to natural daylight/electric lighting (in breakrooms/lunch areas)
findings.consequent: Occupants spend minimum time to maintain healthy circadian rhythm, improved overall health and well-being
findings.mechanism: Provides necessary light exposure for circadian entrainment during breaks, supporting physiological and psychological health.
findings.quote: breakroom and lunch areas can be specifically designed to provide good access to natural daylight or electric lighting. These features can help ensure that occupants spend the minimum amount of time required to maintain a healthy circadian rhythm, leading to improved overall health and well-being.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Implementing the proposed architectural design framework will lead to a measurable improvement in occupants' healthy circadian rhythm, as indicated by EML levels and self-reported sleep quality.

Early integration of circadian lighting design principles (e.g., site analysis, building orientation, material selection) in the design process will result in more effective and cost-efficient circadian lighting solutions compared to late integration.

The use of dynamic lighting systems that mimic natural daylight changes (colder/brighter in morning, warmer/dimmer in evening) will improve occupants' mood, energy levels, and cognitive function in interior spaces.

Interior paint colors with lower melanopic reflectance (e.g., warmer hues) will result in lower melanopic lux levels at night, supporting melatonin production and better sleep, even with fixed light sources.
Seating orientation relative to natural light sources (e.g., skylights) significantly impacts individual melanopic lux exposure and thus circadian rhythm entrainment.

Ongoing education and training for design teams and clients on circadian lighting design principles will increase the successful implementation and effectiveness of circadian lighting systems in built environments.
bridge_warrants: The framework integrates principles from biology (circadian rhythm, melatonin), psychology (mood, perception, cognitive function), and architecture (design process, materials, lighting technology) to create health-promoting environments.
It connects established lighting standards (LEED, WELL) with emerging circadian lighting metrics (EML, CS) to provide a comprehensive design guide.
The framework addresses the interplay between visual comfort and non-visual biological effects of light, bridging traditional lighting design with human-centric approaches.
methodological_critiques: Previous studies on circadian lighting design often miss many elements that affect the non-visual effect of light on humans.

The Color and Illumination Calculator tool relies on user inputs, which can be subject to human error or bias, and does not account for spatial and contextual factors like room geometry, surface reflectance, or natural light.

LEED daylight analysis, by using only average daylight percentages for the whole building, fails to analyze each space individually, thus not guaranteeing sufficient daylight for all occupants' circadian rhythm.
model_structure: The proposed framework is a multi-phase architectural design process, adapted from AIA Integrated Project Delivery (IPD), comprising Predesign & Conceptualization, Ideation & Schematic Design, Detailed Design, Construction Documents, and Post Occupancy. Each phase outlines emergent questions, relevant knowledge domains (Priori, Explicit, Tacit, Procedural, Posteriori), illustrative case studies, and facilitating tools. The framework emphasizes iterative design, continuous education, and collaboration among stakeholders to integrate circadian lighting design effectively.
limitations: The study did not examine the economic aspects (financial implications, energy savings, payback period) of circadian lighting systems due to time constraints.
The impact of dynamic lighting on occupants' perceptions of space was not fully explored.
The framework and findings may have limited generalizability, being specific to the context and scope of the conducted research.
There is a lack of empirical validation for the framework, requiring further studies to enhance its reliability and practical applicability.
The study acknowledges a lack of expertise among designers in incorporating circadian lighting design, highlighting a need for further investigation into training requirements.
The field of circadian lighting design is continuously evolving, meaning the framework may require regular updates to incorporate new research and best practices.
External validation of the framework was limited to a focus group of designers, suggesting a need for broader professional and stakeholder involvement.
The study primarily focuses on architectural projects, and its transferability to other domains or disciplines beyond architecture needs further investigation.
Measuring new material's spectral data was beyond the scope of this research.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Human health and well-being are significantly influenced by the entrainment of circadian rhythms to environmental light-dark cycles, mediated by non-visual photoreceptors.
Architectural design elements can be intentionally manipulated to create indoor light environments that support healthy circadian rhythm entrainment.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural design features influence indoor light exposure patterns, which in turn modulate circadian rhythm entrainment, leading to downstream physiological effects such as immune system regulation.

steps.from_construct: Architectural design features (e.g., window design, artificial lighting systems)
steps.to_construct: Indoor light exposure patterns (e.g., intensity, spectrum, timing)
